common_name: Marquis Wheat (Historic Canadian Hard Red Spring Wheat)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast as soon as spring soil can be worked; young Marquis wheat shrugs off light frost and grows quickly through the cool spring weeks before summer heat sets in.

directions: Marquis was bred by a Canadian agronomist from a Red Fife and Hard Red Calcutta cross, and released around 1909-1910 as a spring wheat that matured one to two weeks earlier than Red Fife while keeping its outstanding bread-baking strength. That earlier ripening let wheat farming push much further north and west across the Canadian Prairies and the U.S. Northern Plains, and by 1920 Marquis accounted for the great majority of hard red spring wheat grown on the continent. Sow it in early spring into a firm, fertile seedbed; it performs best where summers are not too long or humid, ripening ahead of the worst rust and heat pressure. Because it was never patented, home millers and small grain growers can still source and replant true Marquis seed today as a living piece of agricultural history.

common_name: Oberkulmer Rotkorn Spelt (Swiss Heirloom Winter Spelt)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in mid-fall into lean, unamended ground; unlike most modern grains, Oberkulmer spelt actually lodges and underperforms on rich, heavily fertilized soil.

directions: Oberkulmer Rotkorn is a Swiss landrace spelt prized for its genetic purity, having never been crossed back into common bread wheat the way many modern spelt lines have. It grows quite tall, easily reaching five to six feet, and is deliberately grown lean: skip added compost or fertilizer, since excess nitrogen and rich soil cause this old variety to lodge before harvest. Sow into weed-free ground in mid-fall so plants overwinter as a low rosette, then resume growth in spring and ripen for a late-summer harvest. The red-husked grain threshes with more effort than free-threshing wheat because the tough hull clings to the kernel, but it rewards the work with flour that heritage bakers describe as unusually flavorful and easy to digest.

common_name: Kanota Oat (Heirloom California Red Spring Oat)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into cool, workable spring soil as early in the season as the ground allows; Kanota is a quick, early-maturing spring oat rather than a fall-sown type.

directions: Kanota is an open-pollinated red spring oat released in California in 1928 that has stayed in circulation among small grain growers and homesteaders ever since, valued for maturing only a few days behind the earliest oat varieties available. Broadcast or drill seed into firm, cool spring soil and rake it in shallowly for even emergence; the crop grows into a tall, leafy stand that heads out and ripens well before summer heat and humidity peak, which helps it dodge some of the rust and mildew pressure that hits later-maturing oats. Because Kanota is more susceptible than modern varieties to crown rust, stem rust, powdery mildew, and barley yellow dwarf virus, it is best suited to smaller-scale, closely watched plantings rather than large monoculture fields. Harvest when the panicles are fully dry and golden, then thresh and store the hulled grain for rolling, milling, or replanting.

planting.note: Sow in early spring around the last frost date; Purple Karma is a spring-planted barley, hardier than a warm-season crop but less winter-tolerant than fall-sown cereal rye or winter wheat.

directions: This six-row hulless barley traces back to a single seed sample collected in Tibet in 1924 and deposited in the USDA seed repository, where it sat unnoticed for decades before researchers rediscovered and propagated it under the name Karma. Its deep purple-black kernels carry an anthocyanin-rich bran layer, and because the hull is only loosely attached, most of it falls free during ordinary threshing rather than requiring a pearling mill. Sow in early spring into well-drained soil; the plant is notably drought-tolerant once established and performs well on modest, low-input ground. Harvest when heads are fully dry and kernels are hard, then thresh and winnow to reveal grain that cooks up chewy and nutty, similar to pearled barley but with substantially more fiber, zinc, and B vitamins than hulled white barley.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant into flooded paddy beds after all danger of frost, in a long, warm growing season; Wehani needs more heat and time than short-season rice types like Duborskian.

directions: Wehani was developed over roughly a decade by a California rice-growing family, working from basmati-type parent stock, and its name is drawn from the initials of five family members. It is grown as a whole-grain (brown) rice with a reddish-brown bran layer left intact, and it is one of the longer-season aromatic rices, needing a generous warm summer to fill and ripen its large, basmati-shaped grains. Grow it flooded in a paddy bed or lined stock tank, keeping standing water over the root zone through most of the season and drawing it down as the heads dry and color darkens toward harvest. When cooked it releases a toasty, peanut-like aroma that has made it a favorite in home rice blends and pilafs.

common_name: Kokuho Rose Rice (Heirloom California Medium-Grain Rice)

planting.note: Direct sow into a warm, flooded paddy bed well after last frost; this semi-dwarf California variety needs a full, warm-summer season similar to other Central Valley rice types.

directions: Kokuho Rose was bred by a family rice farm in California, crossing Japanese short-grain lines with a Middle Eastern long-grain parent to produce a semi-dwarf medium-grain rice with better flavor than the era's standard Calrose. The family has continuously grown and sold it since the 1960s, making it one of the longest-lived named rice selections still in commercial production in the United States. Grow it flooded in a paddy bed or stock tank through the warm season, maintaining standing water while the plant tillers and fills, then draining as the panicles ripen and dry. Cooked grains turn creamy and slightly sticky with a mild sweetness, making this variety a longtime favorite for sushi rice and home rice cookery on the West Coast.

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, the way durum is grown across the northern U.S. and Canadian plains; in mild-winter Mediterranean climates it can instead be fall-sown as a winter annual.

directions: Durum is the hard, amber-grained wheat relative behind the world's pasta, couscous, and semolina, distinct from common bread wheat in the same way emmer and einkorn are distinct, and it fills a market-class gap that no bread-wheat cultivar can substitute for. It carries deep roots in the Fertile Crescent and is well adapted to semi-arid growing conditions, tolerating dry spells better than many bread wheats once established. Sow in early spring into well-drained soil in full sun; the plant grows a stiff, upright stand with prominent awned heads that dry down to a distinctive amber color at harvest. Home millers mostly grind the very hard kernels for semolina or coarse pasta flour rather than standard loaf bread, since durum's gluten behaves differently than that of hexaploid bread wheat.
